lesson.title: Rules That Change Midstream: Working with Piecewise Functions
lesson.summary: This section covers piecewise functions, which apply different formulas over different parts of their domain, and shows how to evaluate them correctly and graph them using a real world shipping cost model.
lesson.body:
Some real processes genuinely follow different rules depending on the situation. A shipping company might charge a flat rate for anything under two pounds, then an additional per-pound rate beyond that. A single smooth formula cannot capture this kind of behavior, so mathematicians use a piecewise function: a function defined by different formulas on different intervals of its domain. Each formula applies only within its stated interval, and the function is still a single function overall, since the intervals never overlap and together they cover the entire domain.

Consider a shipping cost function C, where x is the weight of a package in pounds. Suppose C(x) = 5 for 0 < x <= 2, and C(x) = 5 + 1.25(x-2) for x > 2. The first piece says any package weighing up to two pounds costs a flat five dollars. The second piece says anything heavier costs that same five dollar base plus $1.25 for every pound over two.

Evaluating a piecewise function means first deciding which interval the input falls into, then applying only that formula. To find C(2), check the intervals: 2 satisfies 0 < x <= 2, so use the first piece, giving C(2) = 5. To find C(5), check again: 5 does not satisfy 0 < x <= 2, but it does satisfy x > 2, so use the second piece: C(5) = 5 + 1.25(5-2) = 5 + 1.25(3) = 5 + 3.75 = 8.75. A package weighing 5 pounds costs $8.75 to ship.

Graphing a piecewise function means graphing each formula only over its own interval and paying close attention to the endpoints, since this is where different rules meet. On this shipping graph, the first piece is a flat horizontal segment at height 5 running from just above x = 0 up through and including x = 2, using a closed dot at (2, 5) since that endpoint is included by the inequality x <= 2. The second piece begins immediately after x = 2 and rises with slope 1.25. Since the second formula also evaluates to 5 at x = 2 (5 + 1.25(0) = 5), the two pieces actually meet exactly at (2,5) with no jump, producing a continuous graph.

Not every piecewise function connects this smoothly. If the two pieces disagree at the boundary, the graph has a visible jump, and it is important not to assume continuity, always check both formulas at the shared boundary value before sketching. This habit of checking domain boundaries carefully carries forward directly into later work on limits, where the behavior of a function as it approaches a boundary point from each side becomes the central question.
